name: Pan-Slavism
summary: Pan-Slavism is a nineteenth-century Romantic movement holding that the Slavic peoples share a language family, ancestry and culture and should stand together politically or culturally. It ranged from Austroslav federalism and equal national rights inside the Habsburg monarchy to Russian-led visions of a Slavic union under the Tsar, and from Prague liberals to Orthodox Slavophile conservatives. Its stated core is solidarity and self-determination for Slavs against German, Magyar and Ottoman domination.
scope: The mainstream nineteenth-century movement as documented in Kollár, Šafárik, Palacký and the 1848 Prague Slavic Congress, Štúr, and the Russian Slavophile and Danilevsky strand. Where strands conflict (autocracy versus constitutional federation, Russian leadership versus equality of Slavic nations) answers are 0 or low. Later Yugoslavism, Soviet-era Slavic solidarity and modern Euro-Slavism are excluded. Most economic and social-policy statements were never addressed and are low-confidence inferences.

keyFigures.name: Ján Kollár
keyFigures.role: Slovak poet who formulated Slavic reciprocity and divided the Slavs into four tribes.

keyFigures.name: František Palacký
keyFigures.role: Presided over the 1848 Prague Slavic Congress and led the Austroslav wing.

keyFigures.name: Nikolay Danilevsky
keyFigures.role: Russian author of Russia and Europe, proposing a Slavic union with Constantinople as capital.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Nineteenth-century Pan-Slavism had no health policy; adherents' welfare views ran from paternalist Slavophile to liberal, so no direction can be inferred.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage regulation did not exist as an issue for the movement, and Slavic intellectuals' social views were too varied to infer a side.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Slavophile-leaning Pan-Slavs distrusted Western industrial capitalism and favoured communal village life, though they offered no economic theory of markets.

public-ownership.rationale: Not an issue the movement addressed; the Slavophile attachment to the communal mir points one way while its conservatism points the other.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Pan-Slavism was a national-cultural movement without a tax programme, and adherents ranged from noble landowners to democrats.

unions-good.rationale: Trade unions were not a concern of the Romantic-era Slavic revival; no position can be derived from its stated aims.

property-fundamental.rationale: Slavophiles prized communal landholding while many Austroslav leaders were bourgeois liberals; the movement had no single property doctrine.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Corporate regulation was outside the movement's concerns; Slavophile hostility to industrial capitalism tilts weakly toward regulation but is only an inference.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare states did not exist in its heyday and the movement never took a position on them.

worker-ownership.rationale: Slavophile praise of the village commune resembles collective ownership of land but was never applied to firms, so any answer is inferred.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Terrorism-era surveillance is anachronistic; Russian conservative Pan-Slavs accepted state police power while Austroslav liberals did not.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Never addressed; the movement's romantic-conservative culture suggests mild disfavour, but this is not documented.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The Prague manifesto prizes freedom of speech as a gain, but Pan-Slavs also wanted protection from national insults; nothing specific on hate-speech law.

strong-leader.rationale: Russian-led Pan-Slavs such as Danilevsky backed autocracy, while the Austroslav and Prague Congress wing wanted federal, equal-rights constitutionalism; adherents are split.

state-harmful.rationale: Pan-Slavism aimed at building Slavic national states or federations, and the manifesto demands state forms for national aspirations, so a stateless society is alien to it.

limit-guns.rationale: Gun control was no issue for the movement; no position can be reasonably derived.

empower-police-military.rationale: Danilevsky-style Russian Pan-Slavs favoured a strong imperial military, but the Prague wing stressed civil freedoms; split and undocumented as a general policy.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Inferred from the movement's conservative, religious-romantic social outlook; the sources do not discuss it.

decide-locally.rationale: The manifesto asks for a federation of equal nations rather than centralism, but Russian-led Pan-Slavs wanted a single imperial centre, so the movement splits.

rehabilitation.rationale: Penal philosophy was not a Pan-Slavic issue; liberal and conservative strands would differ.

traditional-family.rationale: Slavophilia and Orthodox-oriented Pan-Slavism valued organic traditional community, so support is inferred, though family policy was not a stated aim.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the Orthodox and Catholic traditionalist culture of its adherents.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not discussed in the sources; inferred from the church-linked traditionalism of the movement.

more-religion-public.rationale: Slavophiles equated Slavdom with Orthodoxy and Cyril and Methodius were central symbols, so religion held a prominent public role, though Catholic Austroslavs framed it differently.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Not an issue in its era; Slavic emphasis on historic oppression by Germans, Magyars and Turks is about national, not racial, injustice.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Inferred from the romantic and religious view of nature and nation; the movement never discussed gender theory.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Pan-Slavism grew from Romantic scholars in philology and folklore who built Slavic identity, and Slavophiles rejected Western cultural imports, making preservation central.

gradual-change.rationale: Austroslav moderates sought reform within the monarchy, but the Prague Left and Štúr wanted a sharper break; the movement is split.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Migration policy as understood today was not discussed by the movement.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The manifesto proposed a European congress of nations, but that was a forum of equals and not a world authority; Pan-Slavs wanted Slavic solidarity more than global governance.

free-trade.rationale: No documented trade doctrine; Slavophile suspicion of the West tilts one way and liberal Austroslavs the other.

nation-first.rationale: Danilevsky held that each cultural type pursues its own destiny and Europe was hostile to Slavs, so adherents put Slavdom's interests before European cooperation.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Russian Pan-Slavism justified war on the Ottomans to free Balkan Slavs from oppression, which is the nineteenth-century form of this argument.

open-borders.rationale: Inferred: a movement focused on national and civilizational boundaries would not favour eventually open borders, though it never addressed the question.

limit-growth.rationale: Slavophiles distrusted industrialization and praised rural life, but did not argue for limiting growth for environmental reasons.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Anachronistic; no basis for a position in the sources.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Slavophile critique of Western rationalism and industrial progress makes technological optimism unlikely, as an inference.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anachronistic; the movement said nothing on nuclear power.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Prague Congress Left sought alliance with German and Hungarian democrats and the 1848 revolutions were the movement's moment, though Austroslav moderates rejected revolution.

experts-over-public.rationale: Scholars (philologists, historians) founded the movement, but no stated view on expertise versus public in policy.

central-planning.rationale: Slavophiles rejected socialism as alien and favoured the organic commune over designed systems; inferred, not directly debated.

socialized-markets.rationale: No such debate in the movement; the mir resembles it only loosely.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Danilevsky wrote as an economist and favoured Russian self-reliance against Europe, which hints at protection, but Pan-Slavism proper had no tariff programme.

state-directs-investment.rationale: No economic programme; imperial Russian strands accepted state initiative while liberal ones did not.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Slavophile veneration of the peasant commune and village life suggests broad smallholding over concentrated capital, inferred.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Slavophiles rejected socialism as foreign; abolishing money was never part of Pan-Slavism.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Slavophile organic community ideas resemble corporatism loosely, but no source states such a programme.

one-party-rule.rationale: The movement had no party-state idea; the Prague manifesto prizes freedom of speech and action, though Russian autocrats would reject pluralism.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Austroslavs were loyal to the Habsburgs, Štúr and Danilevsky looked to the Tsar, and Danilevsky wanted an Orthodox emperor at Constantinople.

democracy-best.rationale: Modern Euro-Slavism favours democracy and the Prague Left allied with democrats, but Russian Pan-Slavs backed autocracy; the strands split.

direct-votes.rationale: Not discussed; no strand advocated referendums as a principle.

workers-councils.rationale: Slavophile and Austroslav thinking was nationalist and monarchist-federal, with no workers' councils; the commune is the only distant parallel.

right-to-secede.rationale: The manifesto declares equality of all nations and asks that Slavic peoples in Turkey pursue national aspirations in state form, which implies a right for peoples to leave multinational empires.

natural-rulers.rationale: The manifesto rejects privileges and prerogatives of class, but Slavophile conservatives accepted tsarist hierarchy.

political-violence-never.rationale: Russian Pan-Slavs endorsed war against the Ottomans and the movement's 1848 wing joined revolutions; pacifism was not a doctrine.

war-builds-character.rationale: Danilevsky saw conflict between cultural types as natural, but the glorification of war for character is not documented as a Pan-Slavic claim.

separate-church-state.rationale: Slavophiles saw the Orthodox Church as more significant than the state and tied Slavdom to Orthodoxy, which is far from strict separation.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Orthodoxy was central to Slavophilia but laws were not to be drawn from scripture literally; Catholic and Protestant Slavs also took part.

private-courts-defense.rationale: A movement aimed at Slavic statehood and military liberation would reject private provision of defence and justice.

military-superiority.rationale: Russian Pan-Slavs wanted a strong empire to liberate the Balkans, but Austroslavs sought federation, not rivalry; inferred.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Pan-Slavism built on shared language and Slavic identity, and the Prague Congress aimed at national autonomy for Slavic peoples, though Austroslav states were multi-ethnic.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The movement saw history as national and cultural struggle, and the manifesto frames oppression in terms of nations, not classes.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The manifesto demands equality before the law but says nothing on outcomes.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Anachronistic and outside the movement's concerns.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Not discussed; Slavs saw themselves as victims of German, Magyar and Ottoman domination, but did not raise reparations.

civilizational-union.rationale: Uniting Slavs under common language, Orthodoxy or shared culture is the movement's core aim, with Danilevsky proposing a Slavic federation round Constantinople.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Sobornost and organic unity opposed individualism in Slavophile thought.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Slavophile sobornost put communal unity above individualism; the Prague manifesto's rights language balances this, so only low confidence.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Romantic nationalists revered the Slavic homeland and folk tradition, but the sources give no environmental ethic, so the answer is neutral.

limit-population.rationale: Not discussed; a nationalist movement worried about demographic weight would not support limits, but this is undocumented.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Slavophiles opposed industrialization and urban development, but a claim that it is a disaster for humanity goes beyond what is documented.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Slavophile preference for rural life and mistrust of Western rationalism points against disruptive acceleration.

human-enhancement.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the traditionalist outlook.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Anachronistic; Slavophile rejection of Western rationalism suggests opposition.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Encryption postdates the movement by a century and the sources give no basis for a side.

restore-past-order.rationale: Slavophiles idealized pre-Petrine Russia while Austroslav liberals looked forward to federal equality; adherents split.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The movement was a romantic ideology, but Austroslav moderates were pragmatic; nothing documented.

direct-action.rationale: The movement worked through congresses, scholarship and diplomacy more than mass direct action, though 1848 had barricades.

means-match-ends.rationale: The sources show no doctrine linking methods to the intended society; strands used congresses, scholarship, diplomacy and war.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Entirely foreign to a movement dedicated to building Slavic civilization and states.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Not part of any Pan-Slavic doctrine; inferred rejection.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The commune embodied some sharing, but Pan-Slavism had no distribution doctrine.

production-for-use.rationale: Production principles were not part of the Slavic revival, and the Slavophile commune offers only a loose parallel.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Slavophiles rejected socialism as alien, so the labour theory of exploitation was not theirs.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Slavophiles rejected socialism as foreign and the movement was nationalist and monarchist or federalist; class dictatorship is wholly outside it.

collective-farming.rationale: Slavophiles praised the mir's communal land, but that is a village institution, not state-imposed collectivization.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Danilevsky explained conflict by civilizational rivalry between Europe and Slavdom, not by capitalism.

taxation-theft.rationale: A movement aimed at state-building and imperial or federal power did not question the legitimacy of taxation; inferred from its statism.

harm-principle.rationale: The manifesto champions liberty, but Slavophile and conservative strands did not accept a harm-only standard.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The movement rested on the rights of nations and peoples, and the manifesto speaks of equal rights of all nations regardless of power.

conscription.rationale: Russian imperial Pan-Slavism relied on conscript armies and national liberation wars; inferred, not a stated demand.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Pan-Slavs sought to bind peoples through unity and not to rely on emigration as a check; inferred.

state-as-business.rationale: A romantic-nationalist movement did not see states as service firms.

positive-liberty.rationale: The manifesto treats freedom as legal equality and national rights; positive-liberty doctrine is not stated.

media-academia-power.rationale: Intellectuals and scholars created Pan-Slavism, but it did not argue that they outrank elected officials.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Pan-Slavism stressed language and culture; Danilevsky compared cultures to biological species, but race-ability claims are not documented.

organic-representation.rationale: Some Slavophiles favoured Zemsky Sobor-style assemblies of estates and communities, though others favoured autocracy or liberal constitutions.

total-state.rationale: Slavophiles gave the church and the commune weight beside the state, and Austroslavs wanted federalism; no total-state doctrine.

national-rebirth.rationale: Pan-Slavism sprang from a Romantic revival of Slavic nations long under foreign rule, and Danilevsky cast Slavs as a young culture with a future.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Russian-led Pan-Slavism justified expansion in the Balkans and Danilevsky proposed uniting the Slavic world under Constantinople, though the Prague wing opposed domination.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Not discussed; dynastic loyalty to the Tsar or Habsburgs was not feudal personal fealty.

bound-labor.rationale: Most Slavophiles supported the emancipation of the serfs and saw serfdom as a harmful Western-type influence.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The movement's scholars saw themselves as recovering objective Slavic history and philology; no theory of knowledge and power is documented.

universal-morality.rationale: Slavophiles distinguished Russian mystic knowledge from Western rationalism, while Danilevsky denied universal civilization; the Prague manifesto invokes a divine law, so mixed.

single-common-good.rationale: Sobornost expressed unity over competing interests, but this is inferred for Pan-Slavism generally.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Diaspora return rights were never raised; Pan-Slavs thought about Slavs living in neighbouring empires, not emigrant communities.

revive-national-language.rationale: Philologists revived and codified Slavic literary languages, such as Štúr's Slovak standard, and Interslavic grew from the idea of a shared Slavic tongue.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Company governance was outside the concerns of the Romantic-era Slavic revival, and no strand addressed it.

school-vouchers.rationale: Schooling mattered for language revival, but vouchers and school choice are a modern policy the sources never touch.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy was not part of Pan-Slavic thought, and the sources contain nothing on budget deficits.

economic-freedom.rationale: Not discussed; the manifesto links freedom to political rights.

rule-by-example.rationale: The sources record no view on moral example versus law; autocratic and constitutional strands would differ.

national-self-determination.rationale: The manifesto declares full equality of all nations irrespective of size or power and asks for Slavic national rights, which is the movement's founding claim.

force-without-un.rationale: Anachronistic; Russian Pan-Slavs backed Balkan wars without any international sanction.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Slavophiles preferred Russian mysticism and Orthodox faith to Western rationalism.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Welfare for immigrants was not an issue in the nineteenth century, and the sources give no position.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Work requirements for benefits are a modern debate absent from the movement's sources.

class-collaboration.rationale: The organic unity of sobornost and national solidarity across ranks implies cooperation over class conflict, inferred.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Slavic revival was built on recovering heritage in folklore, history and philology, and Slavophiles prized pre-Western tradition.

dominated-front.rationale: Danilevsky described Europe as hostile to Slavdom and urged Slavs to stand against it, and Slavophiles cast the West as the alien rival.

workers-nation.rationale: Workers were not a concern; nation outranks class in the movement but no organizing doctrine is stated.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Not documented; adherents were conservative but the movement itself was silent.

ban-interest.rationale: Usury bans were not a Pan-Slavic demand, and the sources on its economics are silent.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The manifesto demands equal rights and unconditional equality before the law for all nations, which segregation violates.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The movement saw the state as the vehicle of national aims and rejected class-war theory.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Energy policy is anachronistic for a movement of the 1830s to 1880s and the sources offer nothing.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Not discussed; Pan-Slavs resisted forced Germanization and Magyarization of Slavs, hinting against coerced assimilation in general, but no stated position on immigrants.

elite-replacement.rationale: This modern conspiracy theory is not part of Pan-Slavism.

proportional-representation.rationale: Electoral system design was not discussed by Pan-Slavs, whose demands concerned national rights and federation.

national-mission.rationale: Danilevsky cast the Slavs as a kind of Messiah among cultures, but with a distinct culture that should not be imposed on others, so only a qualified yes.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Inferred from the conservative outlook; the sources do not discuss it.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The sources show no populist critique of elites; Pan-Slavs were themselves mostly scholars, nobles and officials.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenics is not part of Pan-Slavism; inferred rejection from its religious culture.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Accountability for past security-force abuses is not discussed; the manifesto only protests violence against Slavs by Hungary.

night-watchman-state.rationale: A movement seeking to build or reshape states for Slavic unity did not favour minimal government, though it had no welfare programme.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Pan-Slavism concerned Slavic peoples sharing language and culture, and some Serbian intellectuals hoped to unite Catholic, Muslim and Orthodox South Slavs; race-purity doctrine is not documented.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The manifesto calls liberty the most sacred right and demands unconditional equality before the law, though its focus is on nations.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Slavophiles rejected socialism as alien, so the issue is foreign to Pan-Slavism.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The movement never debated settler colonialism; Pan-Slavs talked about domination of Slavs by neighbouring powers instead.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The movement spanned Orthodox, Catholic and Muslim Slavs and never addressed civil codes.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Štúr's programme included Orthodox conversion but no law restricting it was proposed.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: This is a question about Hindu practice that has no counterpart in Slavic thought, and sources are silent.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Orthodoxy-linked Slavophilia favoured religion in public life; inferred.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A Marxist doctrine outside the movement's frame.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The manifesto grounds legitimacy in the equal rights of nations and against rule by force and privilege, though Russian autocratic strands would not state it so.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist trade balance goals were not part of the movement's documented programme.

population-transfer.rationale: The manifesto condemns violent methods against Slavic minorities in Hungary and calls for equal rights, but wartime expulsions are not discussed.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Pan-Slavism backed liberation wars and Russian expansion, so it does not hold that initiating force is always wrong.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Danilevsky saw history as rivalry between cultural-historical types, which fits a view that struggle among peoples matters, but not in a progress-focused sense.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Party bans were not discussed, and strands from liberal to autocratic would answer differently.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The manifesto rejects dominance of one nation over another by force and privilege, which is a non-domination idea applied to peoples.

separated-powers.rationale: Constitutional Austroslavs and Zemsky Sobor admirers might favour it, while autocratic Russians would not.

vanguard-party.rationale: Rejected as a socialist idea, which Slavophiles saw as alien.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Orthodox charity ethics are not a stated Pan-Slavic policy.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Council housing is a twentieth-century British policy outside the movement's world, so no position is derivable.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Strikes were not a movement concern, and the sources give no hint of a position.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Malthusian explanations of poverty are not discussed in the sources on Pan-Slavism.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Pan-Slavs stressed Slavic cohesion, but the manifesto and Austroslav plans accepted a federation of many nations.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Not part of the movement; inferred opposition.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Not discussed; Russian-centred strands were more tolerant than Prague liberals.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Price controls were not discussed, and the movement had no economic programme to infer from.

party-controls-media.rationale: The manifesto lists freedom of speech and action as hard-won gains, though Russian conservatives accepted censorship; most adherents would not favour party control.

party-commands-army.rationale: Party armies were not part of the movement; armies belonged to monarchs or states.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Naturalization rules were not a concern of the movement, and the sources offer no basis for an answer.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Pay of representatives was not discussed; the movement's leaders were mostly notables and scholars.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: The Slavic revival had congresses and societies, not disciplined parties, and the sources do not address party discipline.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Pan-Slavism sought union or federation of Slavic states, and modern Euro-Slavism favours Slavic cooperation inside the EU, which involves pooling sovereignty.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Autocratic and Habsburg-loyal strands centred power in the monarch; the Prague liberal wing is not documented either way.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Orthodox-linked Slavophiles favoured episcopal church order; Catholic Slavs likewise, inferred.

clerical-rule.rationale: Slavophiles valued the church over the state but not rule by clerics.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: A nationalist movement would not call for defeat of its own state, and Pan-Slavs supported Russia's wars for the Slavs.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Conservative Slavophiles and Leontiev leaned that way, but Prague liberals defended free speech.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Presidential term limits were not at issue for a movement thinking in terms of monarchs and federations.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall of officials was not discussed; the sources show no strand advocating it.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Pan-Slavism promoted Slavic alliance and solidarity, such as the 1848 congress against German and Hungarian ambitions.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Not discussed; no basis in its sources.

people-in-arms.rationale: The 1848 movement had national guards and volunteers, but the sources do not take a position on replacing professional armies.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Slavophiles praised rural life and opposed industrialization and urban development.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Pan-Slavs sought to unite Slavs across Habsburg, Ottoman and Russian borders, and Yugoslavism united South Slavs.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Not documented; the movement itself was led by educated scholars.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Danilevsky held that cultural types are distinct and cannot pass culture to others, but did not call them equal, and the manifesto affirms equality of nations; the movement splits.

death-penalty.rationale: Slavophiles viewed capital punishment as a harmful Western influence, but others in the movement are undocumented.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from conservative religious outlook.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Evolution teaching was not a live issue in Pan-Slavism's era and sources are silent.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Inferred from traditionalist outlook; not discussed.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: The sources do not address citizenship law, though Slavic identity as such rested on shared language and ancestry.

minority-language-support.rationale: The manifesto demands equal national rights, including for Slavic nationalities in Austria and Hungary to have the same standing as Germans and Magyars.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Exemptions from general laws for religious minorities were not discussed in the sources.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Sobornost valued organic unity over individualism.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: International debt politics is anachronistic for the movement, and the sources give no basis for a position.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Not discussed; political and cultural independence was the aim.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The 1848 congress sat among constitutional revolutions, and Slavs demanded federal reform, but nothing states constituent assemblies explicitly.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Development dictatorship is a modern argument; the sources on Pan-Slavism do not discuss trading freedoms for growth.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Aid duties are a modern question; Pan-Slavs focused on Slavic solidarity, and the sources show no wider stance.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear weapons postdate the movement entirely, so nothing in the sources supports an answer.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Monarchist and imperial strands preferred a ruling dynasty, inferred.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Central bank independence is a twentieth-century question outside the sources.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: The sources do not address trading territory for peace deals; Pan-Slavs argued from kinship, not peace settlements.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Slavophile communal ideas suggest this, but property doctrine is not stated.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental risk policy is anachronistic, and the sources on the movement say nothing.

collective-defense.rationale: Pan-Slavs sought Slavic solidarity against outside powers, and Russia cited it to defend Balkan Slavs.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: The manifesto rejects partition of lands regardless of their peoples, which implies annexation without consent is illegitimate, though Russian Pan-Slavs annexed freely.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Slavophiles saw the church as more significant than the state, which opposes subordinating it.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Monarchist strands see the ruler as above factions, inferred.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: The movement itself sought self-rule for Slavs leaving multinational empires, though some Pan-Slavs resisted Polish separation.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Palacký's delegation asked Austria to become a federation of equal nations, in which each keeps its own institutions.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Autocratic Slavophiles gave the Tsar a religious aura, but divine descent is not part of Slavic doctrine.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax structure was not part of the movement's programme, so the sources give no direction.

character-from-environment.rationale: Not discussed; the movement emphasized inherited language and culture.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Right-wing Slavophiles and Danilevsky accepted autocracy, but Prague liberals demanded equal rights under law, so the strands split.

space-expansion.rationale: Spaceflight is anachronistic for a nineteenth-century movement, and no position is derivable from the sources.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Some Slavophiles favoured a monarchy with consultative assemblies, but it was not a stated doctrine.

leader-cult.rationale: Not discussed; tsar-worship existed in some Russian circles, but it was not a Pan-Slavic principle.

equal-parenting.rationale: Custody law is a modern question the movement never faced.

land-redistribution.rationale: Slavophiles supported emancipation with peasant land, but the movement had no redistribution programme.

refugee-return.rationale: Return of expelled refugees is not discussed in the sources; Pan-Slavs wrote of Slavs under foreign rule rather than refugees.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The movement sought to unite Slavs across borders, and Russia used Pan-Slavism to justify action for Slavic kin abroad.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Not documented; inferred from the movement's mixed-confession character.

common-currency.rationale: Monetary union was not an element of the movement's programme, although Danilevsky imagined a federation; the sources do not mention currency.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Uniting peoples of Slavic language and ancestry across borders is the movement's definition: Kollár's four tribes and Danilevsky's Slavic union.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Austroslavs wanted Slavic autonomy and equal national rights within the Habsburg monarchy.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Not directly relevant; the manifesto demands equal rights for Slavs where they live, but no position on emigration.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Pan-Slavism explained history through nations, language and cultural-historical types, not modes of production.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition policy was not a Pan-Slavic concern and the sources provide no position.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bailouts are a modern financial-policy question the sources do not touch.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Judicial review versus majority will was not at issue; the movement's liberal and autocratic wings would split.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Danilevsky wanted Slavic independence from Europe, but a closed colonial bloc is not documented.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Trade-agreement standards are a modern question with no counterpart in the movement.

moral-incentives.rationale: Work incentives were not discussed in the sources on Pan-Slavism.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The sources describe no theory of small armed groups making revolution; 1848 activity was mass and congress-based.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The manifesto rejects privileges and prerogatives of class, but monarchist and conservative Slavs supported nobility and dynasties; the movement splits.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Slavic scholars built history and folklore to form a Slavic identity, and Danilevsky held cultures to be distinct types.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Russian Pan-Slavs saw Russia as leading smaller Slavs, but the Prague wing rejected domination; Danilevsky said cultures cannot transfer.

patriotic-education.rationale: Romantic scholars aimed to instil Slavic national consciousness, and Štúr's national revival worked through language and schooling.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Admissions preferences are a modern American question outside the movement's sources.

public-money-creation.rationale: Monetary reform was not part of the movement's programme, and the sources are silent.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Capitalist crisis theory is Marxist and was not discussed by Pan-Slavs, so no position is derivable.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Russian Pan-Slavs sought influence in the Balkans and across the Slavic lands, and modern Slavic union advocates echo it.

delink-world-market.rationale: Danilevsky hostile to Europe but no economic delinking is documented.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Marxist concept outside the movement's frame.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The manifesto demands unconditional equality before the law, which leans against allowing discrimination.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The manifesto's emphasis on liberty and equality before the law fits constitutional guarantees, though not stated.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: The manifesto holds that national rights outweigh treaties made by the powers, which fits a rejection of divisions made without consulting peoples.

elective-rulers.rationale: Autocratic and Habsburg-loyal strands favoured hereditary rulers, while liberal Slavs were open to elections.

minority-veto.rationale: Not discussed; a unity-focused movement is unlikely to give individuals vetoes.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The 1848 revolutionary wing resisted Habsburg absolutism, but loyal Austroslavs and Tsarist Pan-Slavs did not.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Liberal Austroslavs favoured constitutional parliaments and right-wing Slavophiles autocracy; split.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal ethics did not figure in the sources on Pan-Slavism.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Animal use regulation was not discussed in sources on the movement.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Paternalism existed among noble Slavophiles but was not a doctrine.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Pan-Slavism was an activist political-cultural movement with congresses and campaigns.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: The critique of mass culture is a twentieth-century theory absent from Pan-Slavic sources.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: A Gramscian idea outside the movement.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Dependency theory is anachronistic; Pan-Slavs saw domination as national, not economic, and the sources give no economic analysis.

native-born-offices.rationale: The sources record no position on reserving offices for natives, though the movement did seek Slavic participation in Habsburg offices.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Danilevsky favoured Slavic independence from Europe, but no development doctrine was stated.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Not discussed; Slavic unity claims were not framed as restoring lost wars' territory.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Postcolonial indigenous leadership is not a topic in the movement's sources.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Fascism arose after the movement's heyday, so the sources provide no basis for a view.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: The comparison of fascism and communism is a twentieth-century debate absent from the sources.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: A movement devoted to national heritage would preserve monuments, inferred.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Men's issues policy is a modern debate not covered by the sources.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Domestic violence policy is outside the movement's sources.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Danilevsky argued each cultural type has its own forms and that Peter's Western reforms were doomed, and Slavophiles said the West's institutions did not fit Russia.

military-guardian-role.rationale: A political guardian role for armies was not discussed; Pan-Slavism's Russian wing had a military ally in the imperial army, but not as constitutional guardian.

paid-care-work.rationale: Wages for housework is a twentieth-century idea unconnected to the sources.

office-by-exam.rationale: The sources do not address civil-service selection, though Habsburg Slavs sought access to state posts.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Foreign ownership of strategic firms was not discussed; the sources give no economic policy.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Binding mandates for delegates were not discussed; the congress was a loose assembly with no such rule.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension design is a modern issue, and the sources give no basis for a view.

land-use-tenure.rationale: The Slavophile commune held land communally with use-based allotment, which resembles this, but it was Russian rather than pan-Slavic.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Liberal strands favoured it, autocratic ones did not.

single-official-language.rationale: The manifesto demands equal national rights and Slavic scholars revived minority languages against German and Magyar dominance, though Russian strands treated Ukrainians and Belarusians as Russians.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Land ownership by foreigners is not covered by the sources, even though Slavs resented German and Magyar landlords.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Disparate-impact doctrine is modern American law and is absent from the sources.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Slavophile critique of Western materialism and industrial life, inferred.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Russian Pan-Slavism supported Balkan Slavic uprisings against the Ottomans.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Not discussed; the Prague wing opposed domination while Russian strands accepted it.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: NGO funding limits are a modern question; the sources show no equivalent position.

corporate-influence.rationale: Lobbying and campaign finance are modern concerns outside the movement's sources.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: The sources do not discuss birth-rate policy.

residents-only-property.rationale: Local limits on property purchases were not discussed by the movement.

job-guarantee.rationale: Employment guarantees are a modern welfare idea absent from the movement's sources.

democratic-peace.rationale: The theory is a twentieth-century political-science claim, and the sources give no position.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Sobornost and loyalty to throne or church suggest duty to obey, though the manifesto is mainly about national rights.

non-intervention.rationale: Russian Pan-Slavism justified intervention against the Ottomans for Balkan Slavs, so strict non-intervention is rejected.

industrial-unions.rationale: Trade union structure was not discussed in the sources on Pan-Slavism.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Conspiracy theories were not in Pan-Slavism's programme, though Pan-Slavs accused Germans and Magyars of hostile design.

public-access-to-information.rationale: The manifesto values freedom of speech, but information-access laws are anachronistic.

local-production.rationale: Slavophile village-centred life hints at it, but no doctrine.

informal-organisation.rationale: The movement used congresses and formal societies.

national-law-over-international.rationale: The manifesto places national rights over treaties, but also proposes a European congress of nations.

religious-nation.rationale: Slavophiles equated Slavdom with Orthodoxy, though Catholic and Muslim Slavs complicated it.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Russian-led strands wanted deference to Russia, while Poles and the Prague congress rejected it.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Fiscal federalism within the Habsburg or Slavic federation was not detailed in the sources.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: The distinction between personal and productive property is Marxist and is not discussed by Pan-Slavs.

defeat-communism.rationale: Anachronistic; Slavophiles rejected socialism as alien but Slavic communist unity arose later.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Public service delivery models are a modern question outside the sources.

religion-illusion.rationale: Slavophiles held Orthodoxy to be the essence of Slavic and Russian identity and rejected Western rationalism.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Slavophile critique of industrialization and Western materialism, inferred.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The sources on Pan-Slavism do not discuss women's equality or its economic conditions.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Slavic revivalists built national and pan-Slavic literary language, and Interslavic is derived from Slavic roots.

treaties-binding.rationale: Treaty rights of nations within a state were not discussed, though the manifesto holds national rights above treaties between powers.

cooperative-communities.rationale: The mir resembles it, but Pan-Slavism sought nations and states, not small communities.

majority-settlement.rationale: Settlement policy toward minority regions was not discussed; the manifesto instead protests Magyar methods against Slavs.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Slavophiles saw a distinct Slavic path between Western capitalism and socialism, but this is general rather than a programme.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Pan-Slavs invoked ancient Slavic homelands, but treated rival claims by Poles and others as contested.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Not part of Pan-Slavism; the sources record no such claim.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The sources on Pan-Slavism are silent on the subject, and adherents' legal views are not documented.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The manifesto prizes freedom of speech, though autocratic strands tolerated suppression.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Orthodox-aligned strands might, Catholic and liberal ones differ.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The manifesto condemns dominance of one nation over another, though Russian expansion was accepted by Pan-Slavs.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Not Slavic; the movement opposed the Ottomans.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Rebellion against rulers who ignore religious law was not part of the Orthodox or Catholic Slavic sources consulted.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Direct participation in workplaces and communities was not a Pan-Slavic theme, and the sources give no position.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Intersectionality is a modern framework with no counterpart in the sources.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Legal gender recognition is a modern question absent from the sources, with nothing to infer from.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The movement spanned Austroslav liberals and Russian conservatives, but never framed it this way.

alienated-labor.rationale: Slavophile critique of Western industrial life resembles it, but not a doctrine of alienated labour.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Pan-Slavs fought the Ottomans, but some Serbian intellectuals sought to unite Muslim, Catholic and Orthodox South Slavs; split.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The manifesto speaks of divine law among nations and Slavophiles saw the tsar as anointed, but Prague liberals ground rights in equality.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Workplace agreements are a modern legal question outside the sources.

social-market-economy.rationale: The sources give no economic model for Pan-Slavism, so a mix of market and protection is not derivable.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: A movement of liberation wars and imperial strength would not abolish armies.

rich-first.rationale: Staged development, as in Deng's formula, is outside the sources on the movement.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Pan-Slavism meant alignment with Slavic Russia or Slavic solidarity against German and Ottoman powers.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Austroslavs accepted the Habsburg monarchy and Russian strands the Tsar, but hereditary rule was not a doctrine of the movement and liberal strands wanted constitutions.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Never addressed; inferred only from the Slavophile idealisation of the peasant commune, which is not a credit theory.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Anachronistic; no side can be inferred from a movement without financial policy.

property-franchise.rationale: Liberal Prague delegates favoured wide franchise while Russian Slavophiles backed autocracy and an assembly of the land without election; strands split.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Not discussed by the movement and no position can be inferred.

reification.rationale: A later Marxist concept; Slavophiles criticised Western rationalism and commerce but did not frame it this way.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Not addressed; Slavophile and liberal strands both objected to censorship but did not argue about wealth and press ownership.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Liberal Prague delegates sought constitutional rule, while the Russian Slavophile strand rejected legalism for the autocrat's rule; the strands conflict.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Prague manifesto demanded equal rights for all nations and individuals in the monarchy, though some Slavic nationalists favoured Slavic dominance in their own lands.

open-government-data.rationale: Anachronistic; the movement called for public assemblies and a free press but not for records of government.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Russian Slavophiles were Orthodox and favoured the church's role while Czech and Slovak strands were mixed Catholic and Protestant; no common position.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Not addressed by the mainstream movement, though some nationalist activists boycotted German or Jewish business; adherents split.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Anachronistic; Slavophiles proposed an advisory assembly of the land but not a sortition body.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: The Orthodox Slavophile strand held that the church's tradition was authoritative and the West's rationalism erred; liberal Czech strands were less settled.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Inferred: Slavophile strands praised the peasant commune over capitalism, though other strands did not address wealth.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Anachronistic: the movement never addressed open service by gay people, and its Romantic and religious conservatism would oppose it.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Inferred: Orthodox Slavophiles saw faith as the core of Slavic identity, and Catholic and Protestant Slavs also kept their churches.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Inferred: it was a nineteenth-century national movement that assumed state policing and never proposed abolishing it.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The Prague manifesto sought equal rights for all nations within the monarchy, which fits sharing power between communities, but the sources do not address executive power-sharing.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Inferred: Slavophiles stressed church and communal life over bureaucratic state, but the strands conflict.

term-limits.rationale: Strands conflict: Russian autocrats had no term limits, while Prague liberals backed constitutional government.

vote-delegation.rationale: Inferred: Slavic liberals wanted an individual vote and conservatives wanted an autocrat, so delegable voting fits neither.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Anachronistic: extinction risk was never discussed, so this is inferred from a focus on national struggles.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Inferred: the Orthodox and Catholic churches of the Slavs reserved clerical office to men, and the movement did not challenge it.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Inferred: Slavophile thought defended the patriarchal family, though the Prague liberals' equality language was about nations, not spouses.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Not addressed; strands differed on liberal rights, and the 1848 manifesto speaks of equality for peoples, not foreign residents.

rent-control.rationale: Not addressed; liberal Austroslavs and the Slavophile commune tradition point in opposite directions.

abolish-ip.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the movement's cultural and linguistic focus, which prized national literature, with no stance on legal monopolies.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Not addressed; the liberal and cultural strands preferred voluntary associations, though the Russian strand favoured state-led unity.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Anachronistic; the movement predates nuclear weapons.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Inferred from its aim of freeing Slavs from foreign domination, which implies resisting foreign armies on Slavic soil.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Anachronistic; no recorded stance on state recognition of genocide.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Not addressed; the Slavophile peasant commune favours labour, but liberal strands had no economic doctrine.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Danilevsky expected war to unite the Slavs, and others saw the use of force as legitimate; inferred that adherents reject an absolute ban.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Kollar and Safarik grounded Slavic unity in a common ancient origin and continuous language, as the overview of the movement describes.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the movement's Romantic and conservative cultural outlook.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the movement's traditional social outlook, which treated women as a given category.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Inferred from Romantic nationalism's reverence for national heroes and for sacrifice for the Slav cause; not stated directly in the sources.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Slavophiles and Danilevsky cast Russia and Orthodoxy as a spiritual mission against the West, but the liberal Austroslav strand did not.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Adherents split: the Russian strand centred unity on Russia, while Kollar's cultural reciprocity valued every Slavic nation.

culture-before-state.rationale: Kollar's literary reciprocity and the cultural revival of Slavic languages came first, with political aims following, as the overview describes.

god-not-male.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the Orthodox and conventional religious outlook of the Slavophile strand.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the strand's reliance on Orthodox tradition as authoritative.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The 1848 manifesto demands equality of nations, so economic life held by one majority is inferred to be rejected.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: The 1848 congress and Stur's aims included grouping Slavs, such as those in Hungary, into their own units; the sources do not state this for regions as such.

independent-unions.rationale: Not an issue for the nineteenth-century movement.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Never addressed; strands ran from liberal to conservative Slavophile.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Never addressed; no stance can be inferred.

second-chamber.rationale: The strands disagreed on institutions, from Tsarist autocracy to constitutional federation.

municipal-property.rationale: Slavophiles prized the peasant commune but liberal Austroslavs did not, so adherents were split.

confederal-coordination.rationale: The Austroslav federation of equal nations is not the same as a confederation of towns; Russian strands favoured autocracy. Strands conflict.

family-wage.rationale: Never addressed; no stance can be inferred.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Anachronistic; no stance can be inferred.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Anachronistic; no stance can be inferred.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Anachronistic; no stance can be inferred.

online-anonymity.rationale: Anachronistic; no stance can be inferred.

person-over-state.rationale: Palacký's liberty and equality before the law fit agreement, but Slavophile sobornost and autocracy stress the community; strands conflict.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Inferred: Slavophiles made Orthodoxy and sobornost central, while Austroslav liberals were more secular.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Austroslav federalists wanted entrenched national rights, Russian strands a strong centre; strands conflict.

gm-crops.rationale: Anachronistic; no stance can be inferred.

dense-cities.rationale: Slavophile anti-industrialism and urban liberals pull opposite ways; no stance can be inferred.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Inferred: the movement organised Slavs politically on shared ancestry and language, though 'race' here means the nineteenth-century 'tribe' or people.

racial-pride.rationale: Kollár and the Romantic philologists built pride in Slavic ancestry and culture as the movement's foundation.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Palacký's manifesto favoured peace among nations, but Danilevsky sought Constantinople by conquest; strands conflict.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Shared Slavic language and descent were the basis of the movement's claim that Slavs form a family of peoples, as Kollar and Safarik argued.

communal-electorates.rationale: Inferred from the movement's national-equality aims, which concerned peoples rather than religious communities; Orthodox Slavophiles and Catholic Czechs held no common line on this.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: The movement arose as a defence against German, Magyar and Ottoman domination, and the Prague congress manifesto protested against such pressure on the Slavs.

free-public-college.rationale: Never addressed; the movement's liberal and conservative strands held opposed views on state social policy.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Not an issue for a nineteenth-century movement, and its strands give no direction to infer.

future-generations.rationale: Inferred from Slavophile romantic stress on tradition and the inherited land and community, which favours handing on a patrimony.

women-distinct-values.rationale: The movement did not address gender in politics, and Slavophile and liberal strands differed on women's roles.

arms-reduction.rationale: Inferred from the Prague manifesto's call for peaceful co-operation of nations, though the Russian strand also glorified military strength.

open-diplomacy.rationale: The Prague manifesto appealed to Europe in public, but Russian-led strands used conventional diplomacy; no common position is documented.

capital-controls.rationale: Capital movements were not an issue for the movement and strands differed on economics.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Inferred from the movement's liberal-national strand, which wanted lawful order under a constitutional state; armed national volunteers appeared in 1848 but no doctrine on arms is stated.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Inferred: Pan-Slavs backed wars of Slavic liberation against Ottoman and Habsburg rule, so refusal of such wars would cut against them, though they also hoped for peace among Slavs.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Labour relations were not addressed; Slavophile paternalists and liberal federalists would differ.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Tax credits were unknown to the movement and no direction follows from its aims.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Public borrowing limits were not a concern of the Romantic Slavic revival; no position can be derived.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: The movement targeted imperial domination of Slavs, but a world economic order was outside its scope and adherents were split.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Inferred: the Prague liberal strand sought federal reform of Austria and the Russian strand defended autocracy, so neither favoured smashing the state.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Economic blueprints were never discussed; Slavophile communal ideas (the obshchina) point one way and liberal federalists another.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Ecosystem accounting is anachronistic and was not addressed.

sacred-nation.rationale: The movement treated the Slavic nation as a living cultural-spiritual community with a historic mission, which Slavophile and Romantic writers described in near-sacred terms.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Student loans did not exist as a policy issue and nothing in the movement's aims bears on them.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Inferred from the Prague congress complaint that Slavs in Habsburg and Ottoman lands were ruled and economically held back by dominant German and Magyar nations.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Inferred from Romantic and Orthodox Slavophile belief in a given moral order of the person, though Slavic writers stressed national character more than universal nature.

public-service-media.rationale: Public media did not exist; the movement valued a national press in Slavic languages but took no stand on funding or control.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Inferred from the Orthodox strand's claim to a unique Orthodox truth and from Catholic and Protestant Slavs' own confessions; the movement did not teach religious unity.

farm-price-support.rationale: Inferred from the Slavophile defence of the peasant commune and its distrust of market capitalism.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Anachronistic; nineteenth-century Pan-Slavism had no position on nuclear weapons.

workers-own-party.rationale: Inferred from the movement's cross-class national appeal, which put Slavic solidarity ahead of class politics.

ban-fgm.rationale: Never addressed by the movement; its sources give no basis for a direction.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Never addressed; adherents ranged from paternalist Slavophiles to liberals, so no direction can be inferred.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Inferred from Kollár's idea of Slavic reciprocity and the stress on a shared Slavic language family, though Štúr codified a separate Slovak.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Anachronistic; the sources record no position on pollution liability.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Inferred from the Prague manifesto's stress on liberty and equality before the law, which sits poorly with hereditary customary rulers.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Anachronistic; Slavophile anti-industrial feeling could support environmental concern, but the sources record no stance.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Not addressed; the Prague manifesto stresses equality before the law but says nothing on sentencing.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Inferred as split: the manifesto demanded equality of national languages, while Russian-led strands favoured Russian dominance.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Nineteenth-century Pan-Slavism had no labour-relations policy; no direction can be inferred.

voter-id.rationale: Not an issue for the movement.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Strands conflict: Russian Slavophiles tied the Slavic nation to Orthodoxy, while Austroslavs defended equal national and religious rights in a Catholic-majority empire.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: The Prague Congress manifesto asked for equal rights of nations and constitutional government, while Russian Slavophiles favoured autocracy; adherents split.

premarital-sex.rationale: Inferred from the traditional, patriarchal and religious social outlook of Slavophile and Romantic nationalist thinkers.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Inferred from the Prague Congress's demand for constitutional rights and freedoms in the Habsburg monarchy.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Never addressed; adherents' economic views were too varied to infer a side.

women-suffrage.rationale: Women's suffrage was not raised by the movement; its main thinkers did not address it, so no direction is inferred.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Inferred from Slavophile and Romantic nationalist views that treated Orthodox or Christian faith as part of Slavic culture.

race-social-construct.rationale: Danilevsky and Kollar treated Slavs as a distinct cultural-historical type with common ancestry, which is at odds with seeing group categories as artificial.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Not addressed; gender-equality bodies did not exist and were not discussed by the movement.

missingStatements.text: The peoples of a multinational empire should be reorganised as a federation of equal nations rather than ruled by one dominant nation.
missingStatements.rationale: The Prague manifesto asked the Austrian emperor to turn the monarchy into a federation of nations with equal rights, and rejects dominance of one nation over another.

missingStatements.text: A people's shared language and culture is a sufficient basis for political solidarity across state borders.
missingStatements.rationale: Pan-Slavism rested on the Slavic languages' similarity and shared identity, built by philologists and folklorists, as the basis for unity.

notes: Strands diverge sharply: Russian-led Pan-Slavs (Danilevsky, later Slavophiles) favoured autocracy, Orthodoxy and Russian leadership, while the Prague congress majority favoured Habsburg federalism, liberty and equal rights, and Poles opposed Russian leadership. The profile resolves splits to 0 or low confidence.
